questions.prompt: How do you handle POST, PUT and DELETE in an Express app?
options: Return 200 for everything so clients don't need to check status.
One handler per method and path, express.json() for bodies, and the right status: 201 with Location, 200/204, 204, or 404.
Use app.get with a ?method= query parameter for writes.
Handle every verb in app.all() and branch on req.method, since Express can only register one handler per path, so no extra setup is needed for it to work.

questions.prompt: How do you handle errors globally in Express, and what changed in Express 5?
options: Use window.onerror on the server.
A four-argument (err, req, res, next) middleware registered last; Express 5 sends rejected async handlers there automatically.
Wrap app.listen in try/catch; Express 5 removed error middleware in favour of process-level handlers, which is what the Express docs recommend for production apps.
Register the error middleware first so it can catch everything after it.

questions.prompt: How do you validate request input in a Node.js API?
options: Use TypeScript types, which validate request bodies at runtime.
Check for the presence of fields with if (req.body) only.
Trust req.body when the client is your own front end, since it already validated the form before sending it, which is what the Express docs recommend for production apps.
Validate req.body against a schema (Zod, Joi, Ajv) at the edge, return 400/422 with field errors, pass only parsed data on.

questions.prompt: What makes a good Express route that takes a DTO, validates it and returns a custom error?
options: Parse with a schema, return a stable error shape (code, message, details) with 422, and never leak stack traces.
Throw a string so Express formats the error.
Return 500 for any invalid input.
Send err.stack back to the client so front-end developers can debug faster, with status 200 to keep caches happy.

questions.prompt: How do you return different HTTP status codes from an Express handler?
options: Express picks the status from the body type: objects give 200, strings give 201 and empty bodies give 404, so no extra setup is needed for it to work.
Set res.code = 404 before res.send().
Status codes can only be set in error middleware.
res.status(code).json(body): 200, 201, 204, 400/422, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429 and 500 for their specific meanings.
questions.explanation: `res.status(code).json(body)`. Common set: `200` OK, `201` created, `204` no content, `400/422` bad input, `401` unauthenticated, `403` forbidden, `404` not found, `409` conflict, `429` too many requests, `500` server fault.

questions.prompt: In Express, what is the difference between app and express.Router, and when do you use each?
options: app is the whole application; a Router is a mountable mini-app with its own routes and middleware, one per feature.
app handles GET requests and Router handles POST requests.
Routers run in a separate process for isolation.
Router is the older API replaced by app in Express 5, so new code should register every route on app directly, which is what the Express docs recommend for production apps.
questions.explanation: `app` is the whole application (settings, listen). A `Router` is a mountable mini-application with its own routes and middleware. Use one router per feature and mount it: `app.use("/items", itemsRouter)`. (In NestJS the closer idea is plain controllers versus controllers with extra framework base classes; NestJS keeps controllers as decorated classes.)

questions.prompt: How do you centralize error handling in an Express codebase?
options: Return null from services and check it in each route.
Handle errors in every route with res.status(...).json(...), so each handler controls its own error format, which is what the Express docs recommend for production apps.
Throw an AppError carrying status and code anywhere, and map it in the single error middleware; business code never touches res.
Log errors to console and let Express crash.

questions.prompt: What is structured logging in Node.js, and why use it?
options: Logging only errors, never info or debug.
JSON log objects with fields (level, msg, requestId, userId) that machines can filter, aggregate and trace across services.
Writing logs into the database inside each transaction.
Logging with console.log in a fixed order, which is faster than JSON and easier to search across services, and it behaves the same in Express, Fastify and NestJS.

questions.prompt: How do you write Node.js logs to a file, and what's better in containers?
options: A Pino destination or Winston file transport with rotation; in containers, write JSON to stdout and let the platform collect it.
Node writes logs to /var/log automatically.
Use console.error, which writes to a file by default.
Use fs.writeFileSync on every log call, which is the standard approach and keeps logs in order under load, and that has been the default behaviour since Node 20.
questions.explanation: Pino: `pino(pino.destination("app.log"))` or a transport. Winston: `new winston.transports.File({ filename })`. In containers the better practice is to write JSON to stdout and let the platform collect and rotate it; files need rotation (`logrotate`, `pino-roll`).

questions.prompt: How does an Express middleware stop the request from continuing?
options: It calls next(false), which tells Express to skip the remaining middleware and close the socket.
It sends a response without calling next(), or calls next(err) to jump to the error handler.
It returns false from the middleware function.
It calls res.end() and then next() so logging still runs.

questions.prompt: How do you pass data between Express middleware, including deep in the call stack?
options: process.env, which is request-scoped.
Global variables, because Node handles one request at a time on its single thread.
Cookies set on the response and read back by later middleware.
res.locals or a typed req property between middleware; AsyncLocalStorage for request context deep in the call stack.

questions.prompt: How should a Node.js service read configuration such as a connection string?
options: Store configuration in localStorage.
Read process.env once at startup in one config module, validate it (e.g. Zod), freeze it, and import that object.
Read process.env.X directly in each handler, so changes to the environment apply without restarts, and that has been the default behaviour since Node 20.
Hard-code values and use git branches per environment.

questions.prompt: How do you access environment variables in Node.js?
options: process.env returns typed values such as numbers and booleans, so no conversion is needed.
process.env.NAME (always strings, so convert and validate); --env-file or dotenv in development, secrets from the platform.
Use require('env') to load them.
Node reads .env automatically in every environment.
questions.explanation: `process.env.NAME` (always strings, so convert and validate). Load a `.env` file in development with `node --env-file=.env app.js` (Node 20.6+) or `dotenv`. Production values come from the platform or a secret store; never commit secrets.

questions.prompt: How can a Node.js service reload configuration without restarting?
options: Node reloads configuration automatically on SIGTERM.
Env vars need a restart; for file or remote config, watch it or handle SIGHUP, validate, then swap the reference atomically.
Re-read process.env in a setInterval, since the operating system updates a running process's environment, which is what the Express docs recommend for production apps.
Call require.cache.clear() and re-import everything.

questions.prompt: What are the three ways a Node.js app can read configuration over time (like .NET's IOptions variants)?
options: Through require, import or fetch.
From JSON, YAML or TOML only.
Synchronously, asynchronously, or via callbacks, which is how Node reads every configuration source, and it behaves the same in Express, Fastify and NestJS.
Once at startup (frozen constant), per request (a getter that rereads), or a live watcher that swaps a shared reference.
questions.explanation: Three read strategies: a value read once at startup (frozen constant, like `IOptions`), a value read per request (a getter that rereads, like `IOptionsSnapshot`), and a live watcher that updates a shared reference and notifies subscribers (like `IOptionsMonitor`). Choose by how often it changes and whether in-flight requests may see a change mid-way.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Code First and Database First with a Node ORM like Prisma?
options: Code First generates SQL from TypeScript types at runtime; Database First means writing raw SQL without an ORM, which is why most Node teams standardize on it.
Code First: schema.prisma plus prisma migrate create the database. Database First: prisma db pull generates the schema.
They're Prisma's two pricing tiers.
Database First is only available for MongoDB.
questions.explanation: Code First: you define models in code, and migrations create or update the database (Prisma `schema.prisma` and `prisma migrate dev`). Database First: the database is the source of truth and you generate models from it (`prisma db pull`, `sequelize-auto`). Code First suits new services; Database First suits legacy or DBA-owned schemas.

questions.prompt: How do you define a one-to-many relationship in Prisma?
options: Give both models a list field and Prisma creates a join table, the same way it models many-to-many, which is why most Node teams standardize on it.
Store the child ids as a JSON array on the parent.
The many side holds the foreign key field plus @relation; the one side has a list field. Index the foreign key.
Use a @oneToMany attribute on the parent model.
questions.explanation:
The "many" side holds the foreign key. Index the foreign key.

```prisma
model Author { id Int @id @default(autoincrement())
               name String
               posts Post[] }
model Post   { id Int @id @default(autoincrement())
               title String
               authorId Int
               author Author @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]) }
```

questions.prompt: In Node.js, what's the difference between constructor (factory) injection and method injection?
options: Method injection means monkey-patching module exports at runtime, which is the idiomatic way to inject in Node, and it behaves the same in Express, Fastify and NestJS.
Constructor injection only works with TypeScript decorators.
Factories receive dependencies once; method injection passes them per call, fitting per-call things like a transaction.
Node has no dependency injection, so modules must import their dependencies directly.

questions.prompt: What happens to a request in Express from arrival to response (and in NestJS)?
options: Each request gets a new Node process.
Express runs all route handlers in parallel and sends whichever response finishes first.
Error middleware runs before route handlers to catch errors early.
Middleware runs in registration order, the matching route handler responds; errors skip to error middleware; finish fires after.
questions.explanation: Server receives the request, it passes through middleware in registration order, a matching route handler runs, the response is sent. A thrown error or `next(err)` skips to error middleware. After sending, the `finish` and `close` events fire (useful for logging duration). In NestJS the order is middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, handler, interceptors, exception filters.

questions.prompt: What are the Node.js equivalents of .NET action filters?
options: Array.prototype.filter applied to the response body.
Express has no equivalent, so cross-cutting logic must be copied into every route handler, and that has been the default behaviour since Node 20.
process.on('request') listeners.
Route-level middleware (auth, validation), Fastify lifecycle hooks, or NestJS guards, pipes and interceptors.
questions.explanation: Route-level middleware: `router.post("/items", requireAuth, validate(CreateItem), handler)`. Fastify has lifecycle hooks (`preHandler`, `onSend`); NestJS has guards, pipes and interceptors. Use them for cross-cutting concerns: auth, validation, timing, caching.

questions.prompt: How do you log HTTP requests and responses in a Node.js API?
options: Write a middleware that stores every request in Redis forever.
Log req and res objects in full with console.log, including bodies and headers, for complete audit trails, which is why most Node teams standardize on it.
Log only the URL so logs stay small.
pino-http or morgan: method, path, status, duration, request id; redact secrets and skip bodies by default.

questions.prompt: In Express, what are req.params, req.query, req.body and form data?
options: Path segments, query string, parsed payload (express.json / urlencoded), and multer for file uploads; all untrusted.
They're the same object exposed under four names for backward compatibility.
req.params holds headers and req.query holds cookies.
req.body is parsed automatically without any middleware.
questions.explanation: `params` come from the path (`/items/:id`), `query` from the query string, `body` from the payload (`express.json()` for JSON, `express.urlencoded()` for HTML forms, `multer` for file uploads). All are untrusted strings or objects: validate and convert each.

questions.prompt: Why does middleware order matter in Express, and what's a typical order?
options: It runs in registration order: helmet and CORS, request id and logging, parsers, auth, rate limit, routes, 404, error handler.
Error handlers must be registered first.
Body parsers must run after the routes.
Express sorts middleware by priority internally, so registration order only matters for performance, and it behaves the same in Express, Fastify and NestJS.
questions.explanation: Middleware runs in registration order. Typical order: security headers (`helmet`) and CORS, request id and logging, body parsers, auth, rate limit, routes, 404 handler, error handler. Wrong order gives bugs such as reading `req.body` before the parser, or auth running after a route.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between app-level, router-level and error middleware in Express?
options: App-level middleware only runs once at startup, router-level runs per request, and error middleware runs on 404s, which avoids the overhead of the alternatives entirely.
They're interchangeable; the names describe file locations.
Error middleware runs on every request after the response.
app.use applies to everything, router middleware to one router, and error middleware (4 params) only runs on errors.
questions.explanation: App-level (`app.use`) applies to everything; router-level applies to one router; error middleware has four parameters and runs only when an error is passed. Scope middleware as narrowly as correctness allows.

questions.prompt: How should a Node.js process handle uncaughtException and unhandledRejection?
options: Ignore them; Node retries the failed code automatically.
Convert them into 500 responses for the current request.
Log, flush and exit non-zero so a supervisor restarts a clean process; also handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.
Log the error and keep serving requests, because exiting the process would drop every in-flight request, which avoids the overhead of the alternatives entirely.
questions.explanation: Log, flush and exit with a non-zero code; let the supervisor (Kubernetes, systemd, PM2) restart a clean process. Continuing after an uncaught exception risks corrupt state. Also handle `SIGTERM` for graceful shutdown (stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close DB).

questions.prompt: How do you inject dependencies into a custom Express middleware?
options: Attach dependencies to globalThis at startup, which every middleware can read without imports, so no extra setup is needed for it to work.
Express injects services by parameter name automatically.
Write a factory that takes the dependencies and returns the middleware, so it stays testable and global-free.
Import the dependency inside the middleware on every request.

questions.prompt: For an Express API, when do you return 404 and when 204?
options: 204 when the resource doesn't exist and 404 when a list is empty, since both mean 'nothing found', which avoids the overhead of the alternatives entirely.
Always 200, with an error field when needed.
404 for every DELETE so clients refresh.
404 when the addressed resource doesn't exist; 204 for success with no body; an empty collection is 200 with [].
questions.explanation: `404`: the resource does not exist (GET, PUT or DELETE by id of something unknown). `204`: the request succeeded and there is intentionally no body (successful DELETE or PUT). An empty collection is `200` with `[]`, not 404.

questions.prompt: How do you handle a needed breaking change in a Node.js API?
options: Avoid it with additive changes; if unavoidable, ship a new version, keep the old one, announce dates, watch usage, use contract tests.
Ship it in a patch release and bump the npm package version, which notifies every API consumer automatically, and that has been the default behaviour since Node 20.
Breaking changes are fine if the response stays JSON.
Change the old endpoint in place and document it in the README.
questions.explanation: Avoid it. Prefer additive, backward compatible changes (new optional fields, new endpoints). If a break is unavoidable: ship a new version, keep the old one running, announce deprecation with dates (`Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers), watch usage, and use contract tests with consumers.

questions.prompt: What's the most common way to version a Node.js REST API?
options: In the request body, because GET requests in Express can't carry version information any other way, which avoids the overhead of the alternatives entirely.
With a cookie named api-version.
In the URL path (/v1/items): visible, cacheable, simple to route; headers or a query parameter are the alternatives.
In the package.json version field.
questions.explanation: URL path (`/v1/items`), because it is visible, cacheable and simple to route. Alternatives: a header (`Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json`) or a query parameter. Pick one and be consistent.

questions.prompt: Why map objects by hand between layers in a Node.js service?
options: Spreading the database row into the response is safer, since it keeps every field the client might need, which is why most Node teams standardize on it.
Manual mapping is required because JSON.stringify can't serialize classes.
Explicit conversion functions are type-safe and debuggable, and stop internal fields like password hashes from leaking.
It improves V8's garbage collection.
questions.explanation:
Writing explicit functions that convert between layers (request DTO to domain model to DB row to response DTO). It is verbose but type-safe, easy to debug, and stops internal fields (password hash, internal ids) from leaking. Avoid magic auto-mappers unless the shapes are truly identical.

```js
const toItemDto = (row) => ({ id: row.id, name: row.name, price: row.price_cents / 100 });
```

questions.prompt: Where do most Express APIs sit on the Richardson Maturity Model?
options: Level 2: resources with proper HTTP verbs and status codes; level 3 adds hypermedia links (HATEOAS).
Level 0, since JSON APIs can't be RESTful.
Level 1, because Express doesn't support DELETE.
Level 3, because Express adds hypermedia links to JSON responses automatically when routers are used.
questions.explanation: Four levels of REST adoption: 0 one endpoint, one verb (RPC over HTTP); 1 resources with their own URLs; 2 correct HTTP verbs and status codes; 3 hypermedia (HATEOAS: responses carry links to next actions). Most production APIs sit at level 2.

questions.prompt: For a Node.js team, what separates a monolith, a modular monolith and microservices?
options: A modular monolith uses npm workspaces, while microservices use separate git repositories but share one database.
Microservices are monoliths running in cluster mode.
Modular monolith: one deployable with strict module boundaries and no cross-module DB access; microservices deploy and own data separately.
They only differ in the number of Express routers.
questions.explanation: Monolith: one deployable, usually tangled. Modular monolith: one deployable with strict module boundaries and no cross-module database access; cheap to run and a good default. Microservices: independently deployable services with their own data, giving team and scaling independence at the price of network failures, distributed data and operational cost. Split only when a boundary and a reason are clear.

questions.prompt: What does an API gateway do in front of Node.js services, and what's the risk?
options: Routes and handles auth, rate limits, TLS, aggregation, caching; risks are a single point of failure and creeping business logic.
It compiles TypeScript for the services at request time.
It's only needed for WebSocket traffic.
It replaces each service's database with a shared cache and runs the business rules centrally for consistency, so no extra setup is needed for it to work.
questions.explanation: A single entry point in front of services: routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS, request aggregation, caching and observability. It spares clients from knowing the internal topology. Risks: a single point of failure and a place where business logic wrongly accumulates.

questions.prompt: In a Node.js app's database, what is normalization and when do you denormalize?
options: It's lowercasing all string columns.
Store each fact once to avoid update anomalies; denormalize deliberately for read-heavy paths and keep copies in sync.
Normalization means converting rows to JSON documents; denormalize when you need foreign keys, which is why most Node teams standardize on it.
Normalization is done automatically by Prisma migrations.
questions.explanation: Normalization removes duplicated data into separate tables to avoid update anomalies. Denormalize deliberately for read performance (reporting, search, read models, hot lists) and keep copies in sync through events or triggers; measure first.

questions.prompt: Why do indexes speed up a Node.js app's queries, and what does adding too many cost?
options: Indexes only help Prisma, not raw SQL.
Indexes store query results in memory, so they cost nothing and should be added to every column, so no extra setup is needed for it to work.
Indexes speed up writes and slow down reads.
A B-tree lets the database find rows without a scan; each extra index slows writes, uses storage and burdens the planner.
questions.explanation: An index (usually a B-tree) lets the database find rows without scanning the table. Costs: slower writes (every index updates), more storage, and more work for the query planner. Index columns used in filters, joins and sort; check plans with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`; drop unused indexes.

questions.prompt: For a Node.js backend's data store, what does the CAP theorem force you to choose?
options: During a network partition, consistency or availability; partitions happen, so it's CP or AP, often per operation.
Between SQL and NoSQL.
Two of consistency, availability and performance at design time; partitions only matter for multi-region setups, and it behaves the same in Express, Fastify and NestJS.
Between caching and persistence.
questions.explanation: In a network Partition a distributed store must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write) and Availability (every request gets a non-error response). Partitions happen, so the real choice is CP or AP during a partition. Many systems tune this per operation.

questions.prompt: In a Node.js system, how do strong and eventual consistency differ for API design?
options: Strong: readers see every completed write. Eventual: replicas converge later, so design for staleness and idempotency.
Eventual consistency means data is eventually deleted.
Strong consistency is a JavaScript strict-mode setting; eventual consistency is the default in sloppy mode, which is what the Express docs recommend for production apps.
There's no difference once you use await.
questions.explanation: Strong: after a write completes, all readers see it (higher latency, lower availability). Eventual: replicas converge over time, so readers may see stale data briefly (higher availability and speed). Design UX and APIs for staleness (read-your-writes where needed, idempotent updates, conflict resolution).

questions.prompt: How does horizontal versus vertical scaling apply to Node.js specifically?
options: Horizontal scaling requires rewriting the app in worker threads.
One process runs JS on one core, so scale out with several processes (cluster, containers) and keep sessions out of memory.
Node can't run behind a load balancer.
Node uses all cores automatically through the event loop, so vertical scaling is all you ever need, and it behaves the same in Express, Fastify and NestJS.
questions.explanation: Vertical: bigger machine (simple, capped, single point of failure). Horizontal: more instances (needs stateless services, shared or sharded data, load balancing). Node specifics: one process uses one core for JS, so run several processes (cluster, containers) and keep sessions out of memory.

questions.prompt: When would a Node.js service use NoSQL instead of a relational database?
options: Only for read-only data.
By access pattern: massive key lookups, flexible documents, graphs, time series; relational for transactions, joins and constraints.
When the team prefers JSON over SQL syntax.
Always, because JavaScript objects map directly to documents and relational drivers block the event loop.
questions.explanation: Choose by access pattern and consistency needs, not fashion: massive scale and simple key access (key-value, wide column), flexible or hierarchical documents, graph traversals, time series. Stay relational for transactions, joins, constraints and ad hoc queries. PostgreSQL with `jsonb` covers many "flexible" cases.

questions.prompt: What is a distributed lock in a Node.js system, and what are its risks?
options: A file lock, which is always safe on NFS.
A mutex from the async-mutex package, which is safe across servers because it uses the event loop.
A lock across processes (Redis NX PX, advisory locks); expiry mid-work, clocks and split brain mean you need fencing tokens.
A Postgres transaction; the only risk is a slow commit.
questions.explanation: A lock shared across processes (Redis `SET key val NX PX`, Redlock, Postgres advisory locks, ZooKeeper). Risks: expiry while the holder is still working (GC pauses, slow calls), clock assumptions, split brain, and deadlocks. Use TTLs, renew while working, and fencing tokens so the resource rejects stale holders; prefer idempotent operations or queue partitioning over locks.

questions.prompt: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking from a Node.js app: how do you implement each?
options: Prisma does both automatically on every update.
Optimistic: wrap the update in a JavaScript lock; pessimistic: retry until the database stops throwing.
Both need Redis; Postgres can't lock rows.
Pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction. Optimistic: a version column in the WHERE; 0 rows updated means conflict.
questions.explanation:
Pessimistic: lock the row up front (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`); safe under high contention, blocks others. Optimistic: no lock; a version column makes the update conditional and a conflict is retried or reported; best for low contention.

```sql
UPDATE items SET qty = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3; -- 0 rows = conflict
```

questions.prompt: How do you design a multitenant database for a Node.js SaaS?
options: Separate tables named after each tenant in one schema.
One Prisma client per tenant pointing at the same tables, which isolates tenants without any tenant column, which is why most Node teams standardize on it.
Shared tables with tenant_id (plus RLS), schema per tenant, or database per tenant; choose by isolation, compliance and scale.
Store tenant data in browser storage.
questions.explanation: Three models: shared tables with a `tenant_id` (cheapest; enforce with Postgres row-level security and a mandatory tenant filter), schema per tenant (moderate isolation), database per tenant (strongest isolation, highest cost). Decide by isolation, compliance, noisy neighbours and tenant count. Always index `tenant_id` and test for cross-tenant leaks.

questions.prompt: For a Node.js service, how do cache-aside, write-through and write-back differ?
options: Cache-aside fills on miss and invalidates on write; write-through writes both; write-back flushes later and risks loss.
They're Redis eviction policies.
They differ only in TTL length.
Cache-aside writes only to the cache; write-through writes only to the database; write-back reads from both, and that has been the default behaviour since Node 20.
questions.explanation: Cache-aside: the app reads the cache, on miss reads the DB and fills the cache (most common; invalidate on write). Write-through: writes go to cache and DB together (consistent, slower writes). Write-back: write to cache, flush to DB later (fast, risk of data loss). Always set TTLs and plan stampede protection.

questions.prompt: For Node.js services, when do you choose REST, gRPC or GraphQL?
options: REST only; Node can't run gRPC servers.
Always GraphQL, since it replaces both.
REST outside (public, cacheable), gRPC inside (contracts, streaming, low latency), GraphQL for clients shaping their own data.
gRPC for browsers since it's JSON, REST for internal calls because it's binary, GraphQL only for files, so no extra setup is needed for it to work.
questions.explanation: REST: public, cacheable, simple resource APIs. gRPC: internal service-to-service calls, strong contracts (protobuf), streaming, low latency. GraphQL: many different clients that need to shape their own data, at the cost of caching and query-cost control. Often: REST outside, gRPC inside.

questions.prompt: When should Node.js services use a message queue rather than calling each other's APIs?
options: Whenever latency matters, because queues deliver faster than HTTP between services.
Only for logging and metrics.
When the answer isn't needed now: smoothing spikes, decoupled availability, retries, fan-out, long jobs; at the cost of eventual consistency.
Never; queues block the event loop.
questions.explanation: When the caller does not need the answer now: smoothing spikes, decoupling availability, retries, fan-out to multiple consumers, long jobs. Use direct calls when you need an immediate result. Costs: eventual consistency, ordering, duplicates, observability.

questions.prompt: For Node.js consumers, what do at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once mean?
options: They describe how many consumers share a queue.
Exactly-once is achieved with setTimeout retries.
At-most-once may lose, at-least-once may duplicate; exactly-once in practice is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.
At-least-once may lose messages; exactly-once is what kafkajs and amqplib guarantee by default.
questions.explanation: At-most-once: may lose messages, never duplicates. At-least-once: never loses, may duplicate (the usual default). Exactly-once in practice is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing (dedupe by message id); true end-to-end exactly-once is only possible within a closed system such as Kafka transactions.

questions.prompt: Which Node.js messaging libraries would you use, and how do you do idempotency and retries?
options: Use setInterval polling of an HTTP endpoint instead of a broker.
kafkajs/confluent, amqplib, BullMQ, NATS; record processed ids with the effect (inbox), backoff with jitter, retry cap, DLQ.
Idempotency isn't needed if handlers are async.
Any library; retry failed messages immediately in a loop and rely on the broker to drop duplicates, which is why most Node teams standardize on it.
questions.explanation: Libraries: `kafkajs`/`@confluentinc/kafka-javascript`, `amqplib` (RabbitMQ), BullMQ (Redis jobs), NATS, cloud SDKs. Idempotency: carry a unique message id and record processed ids in a table inside the same transaction as the effect (inbox pattern), or use idempotency keys on HTTP writes. Retries: exponential backoff with jitter, a retry limit, and a dead-letter queue; only retry safe or idempotent work.

questions.prompt: How do you apply Clean Architecture's dependency rule in a Node.js codebase?
options: The domain imports nothing from Express or Prisma; it declares ports that adapters implement, wired in one composition root.
The domain extends Prisma models so entities can save themselves.
Every module imports the Express app so it can register its own routes and database access directly, which avoids the overhead of the alternatives entirely.
It means one folder per npm dependency.
questions.explanation: Concentric layers: entities and use cases at the center, adapters (HTTP, DB, queues) outside. Dependencies point inward only: the domain imports nothing from Express or Prisma; it declares interfaces (ports) that outer code implements, wired in one composition root. Benefit: testable core and replaceable infrastructure. Do not apply it ceremonially to a tiny CRUD service.

questions.prompt: Should you wrap Prisma in Repository and Unit of Work classes?
options: Usually not: Prisma already offers repository-like APIs and $transaction; wrap only to shield the domain or ease testing.
Repositories are required for Prisma migrations.
Never use Prisma directly from any code.
Yes, always, because Prisma can't run transactions without a Unit of Work class around it.
questions.explanation: Prisma, TypeORM and Sequelize already implement unit of work and repository-like APIs (`prisma.$transaction`). Wrapping them adds a layer that is worth it only to protect domain code from the ORM or to ease testing; otherwise it is boilerplate. If you do, keep repositories small and aggregate-oriented, and let the use case own the transaction.

questions.prompt: In a Node.js codebase, what is Vertical Slice Architecture and how does it reduce coupling?
options: Giving each developer a vertical layer of the stack.
Each feature keeps route, validation, handler, data access and tests together, so a change stays in one folder.
Splitting the code into controllers/, services/ and models/ folders shared by all features, which avoids the overhead of the alternatives entirely.
Running each feature in its own Node worker thread.
questions.explanation: Organise code by feature (a slice contains its route, validation, handler, data access and tests) instead of by technical layer. Changing a feature touches one folder; slices share little, so coupling between features is low and each slice can choose its own approach.

questions.prompt: How do you organize a Node.js project with vertical slices?
options: src/controllers, src/services and src/repositories, with one file per feature in each folder.
Everything in index.js so imports stay short.
One npm package per HTTP route.
src/features/<use-case>/ with route, schema, handler and tests; a small stable shared/ folder; app.ts mounts the feature routers.
questions.explanation:
A slice per use case, a small shared kernel, and one composition root that mounts each feature's router.

```text
src/
  features/
    create-order/  route.ts  schema.ts  handler.ts  handler.test.ts
    get-order/     route.ts  query.ts   handler.ts
  shared/          logger.ts  db.ts  errors.ts   (small, stable)
  app.ts           (composition root, mounts feature routers)
```

questions.prompt: In a Node.js vertical-slice project, how much duplication between slices is acceptable?
options: Some: extract on the third repetition and share only stable things (errors, logging, auth, a small domain kernel).
Duplication is fine only in tests.
None: extract a shared helper the moment two slices contain similar lines, including their DTOs and queries, and that has been the default behaviour since Node 20.
All of it; slices should never share any code, not even logging.
questions.explanation: Accept some duplication: it is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. Apply the rule of three (extract on the third repetition), and share only genuinely stable things (error types, logging, auth, a small domain kernel). Do not share DTOs or query code between slices just to save lines.

questions.prompt: How do you implement CQRS simply in a Node.js service?
options: CQRS in Node requires event sourcing and two databases from day one, otherwise queries can't scale, and it behaves the same in Express, Fastify and NestJS.
Separate command and query handlers on one database first; add an event-fed read model only when reads need it.
Use a message bus for every query.
Split each route into a GET router and a POST router only.
questions.explanation:
Separate commands (change state, return little) from queries (read only, return DTOs). Minimal version: two handlers per feature and the same database. Fuller version: a separate read model fed by events, which scales reads independently but adds eventual consistency. Start minimal.

```js
const placeOrder = async (cmd) => { /* validate, write, publish OrderPlaced */ };
const getOrderSummary = async (id) => db.orderSummaries.findUnique({ where: { id } }); // read model
```
